Review the conversation context below and respond with a concise summary
of important items that should be preserved in the daily log.
Do NOT use any tools — just return plain text.

Format your response as a structured daily log entry with these sections:

**Context:** [One line about what the user was working on]

**Key Exchanges:**
- [Important Q&A or discussions]

**Decisions Made:**
- [Any decisions with rationale]

**Lessons Learned:**
- [Gotchas, patterns, or insights discovered]

**Action Items:**
- [Follow-ups or TODOs mentioned]

Skip anything that is:
- Routine tool calls or file reads
- Content that's trivial or obvious
- Trivial back-and-forth or clarification exchanges

Only include sections that have actual content. If nothing is worth saving,
respond with exactly: FLUSH_OK

## Conversation Context

**Ask independent questions over the same state together**, including useful

speculative questions. They run in parallel and cannot see one another's answers.

State each speculative premise explicitly; code consumes the applicable answers.

A second request is warranted when an earlier answer is needed to fetch evidence,

construct new state, or determine the next options. Extra questions still use tokens;

measure actual request budgets, cost, and end-to-end latency.



Use probabilities and confidence to guide behavior, with thresholds evaluated on

the user's data and consequences. Choice/Score confidence summarizes distribution

concentration, not overall workflow correctness or permission to act. A Noul near

0.5 means similar probability for yes and no, not medium intensity. Several

acceptable alternatives can also spread probability; low confidence need not

invalidate a harmless preference choice. Ignore uncertainty on unused branches.



Keep policy explicit and raw judgments reusable. Weighted scores suit compensating

preferences; an “any serious violation” rule needs separate conditions. Changing a

weight or display filter need not rerun inference when evidence and question meanings

are unchanged. Typed output guarantees the interface, not truth. System One models

are trained for calibrated decisions; validate their performance in the target domain.



Test representative cases and the resulting application behavior. For failures,

inspect the exact state, questions, candidates, answers, composition, and observed

outcome. Separate missing evidence, model errors, code errors, and service failures.

Treat cookbook thresholds and demo results as examples to evaluate, not universal

rules or permanent model limitations. Keep API credentials server-side in web apps.

**Assistant:** Fetching the TypeSafe intro, and in parallel checking what's in the DEV root and TypeSafe_Sandbox. Your notes say Jev already runs a router and a verifier there, so I shouldn't suggest those again.

**Assistant:** PR #21 (surgery notes) isn't on main yet. I'll check it to see where the surgery item and the other open candidates stand.

**Assistant:** Following the advisor, I'll check two things before writing: how `meeting-prep` and `status-report` currently connect meetings to projects, and what text the screening records hold beyond the title.

**Assistant:** `meeting-prep` finds meetings by searching vault notes for the project's name. Let me confirm how `status-report` assigns meetings to projects, and what fields a screening record carries.

**Assistant:** I checked the last two things. Here is what they showed:

- **`status-report` has no project tag on meetings.** It pulls every meeting in the period, and the drafting pass sorts them into projects by hand.
- **`meeting-prep` step 2 searches vault notes for the project's name.** Per the open PR #21, the exact project name appears in 0 of 279 meetings.
- **Screening records already carry a human-labelled `studyDesign` and an `INCLUDE`/`EXCLUDE` decision.** That gives the study-design idea a ready-made test set.

That's everything I needed. My answer is below.

---

# Where Jev could still help

## Start with what's already been measured

This question was answered yesterday. `TypeSafe_Sandbox/docs/handoffs/2026-09-21-leverage-sweep-all-projects.md` ranked every project for Jev, and each candidate came with a test that could rule it out. Since then:

- **Evidence Library tags failed.** Your blind check came out 60% against a 70% bar, so the rules stay.
- **The surgery-notes probe failed.** It's recorded in PR #21, which is still open.
- **The Fireflies attendee lookup failed** (also in PR #21). That result is what keeps one idea alive, below.
- **Eight ideas have now been measured and dropped.** The sandbox's own recorded advice is "maintenance: keep the skill router and verifier, stop hunting."
- **The DEV root has no code.** It's only the workspace map, so the candidates below come from the sub-projects.

I used the project's own three conditions for a Jev build:

1. The answer is a genuine judgment call, not a lookup, a join, or a threshold.
2. Something already uses the answer.
3. A plain-code approach was tried first and fell short.

Three ideas are left. Only the first one meets all three conditions.

## 1. Tag each Fireflies meeting with its project (recommended)

**Where it fits**
- `meeting-sync` writes meeting notes into the vault inbox with no project on them.
- `meeting-prep` step 2 finds a project's meetings by searching those notes for the project's name.
- `status-report` step 2b pulls every meeting in the period and sorts them into projects by hand while drafting.

**Problem it solves**
- The exact project name appears in 0 of 279 meetings, so `meeting-prep`'s name search can't find them reliably.
- Simple word matching fires on 252 meetings, but 210 of those match more than one project.
- Attendee lookup settles only 6% of meetings (18 of 279). Most meetings have no attendee data at all.

**What we'd send Jev**
- The meeting title plus the Fireflies overview and topics, with people's names removed first. The capability map already requires that.
- The list of chartered projects, one line each.

**The question**
- A **Choice**: "Which of these projects is this meeting mainly about?"
- The options are the five chartered projects plus "none of these." That last option is required: of the 84 meetings with named speakers, 39 pointed at no chartered project.

**How the answer is used**
- `meeting-sync` adds a `project:` line to the note header.
- `meeting-prep` checks that line first and falls back to today's name search.
- `status-report` groups meetings by the tag in its draft, which you still review.

**If it's uncertain, wrong or unavailable**
- Below a confidence cut-off, or on "none of these," the note gets `project: unfiled`. That's the same as today.
- If the service is down, the sync still runs and the note just has no tag.
- A wrong tag costs little: `meeting-prep` still falls back to the name search, and you read the report before sending it.

**How to test it**
- You hand-tag about 40 meetings from July onward before any Jev call.
- Pass bar, written down before the run: when Jev is confident, it's right at least 90% of the time, and it's confident on at least 60% of meetings.
- Then run one real `/meeting-prep` and count the meetings it finds against today's search.

**Honest limits**
- About 3 meetings a week, so the gain is modest.
- Claude already does this sorting while drafting each report. What's new is a tag written once and reused, instead of worked out again every time.

## 2. Identify each paper's study design for the research shortlist

**Where it fits**
- `evidencePriority()` in `SportScienceResearchRepo/scripts/build-pilot-shortlist.mjs` (line 34) scores papers with regex on the title alone.
- The score orders the 1,534 unscreened PDFs for screening.

**Problem it solves**
- 80 of the 197 screened records match no design pattern at all, so good papers can sink in the queue.

**What we'd send Jev**
- The title plus the text of the first page. That text isn't extracted for unscreened PDFs yet, although the screening step already extracts text for the papers it covers.

**The question**
- A **Choice** over the same design labels the screeners use: systematic review/meta-analysis, consensus, RCT, cohort, case-control, cross-sectional, validity/reliability, case report, commentary/editorial, other.

**How the answer is used**
- Code converts the design into the existing weights (12, 10, 9…).
- The sport and population bonuses and the editorial penalty stay as they are, because they match exact words and code handles them reliably.

**If it's uncertain, wrong or unavailable**
- Low confidence or no answer falls back to today's title-regex score.
- A wrong answer only changes screening order. A person still screens every paper.

**How to test it**
- The 197 screened records already have a human `studyDesign` label and an include/exclude decision.
- The fair comparison is regex run on the same first-page text, not on the title alone. Nobody has tried that yet, so code might close the gap by itself.
- Pass bar: Jev beats first-page regex on design accuracy, and its shortlist ranks more INCLUDE papers near the top.

**Caution:** the domain-tag test in this same repo just failed. It also needs text extraction before it can start.

## 3. Rate spring exit notes for development trajectory

**Where it fits**
- `Football/SpringPlayerEvals_SymAnalysis/`. `coach_pdf.py` prints a 1–5 trajectory from `semantic_scores.json`.
- Those scores came from a one-off Claude pass.

**Problem it solves**
- The Claude pass is the best result so far (ρ = +0.30 against PFF snaps), but it can't be rerun the same way.
- The keyword rubric in the spreadsheet scored 0 on 51% of notes.

**What we'd send Jev**
- One athlete's four department notes (position coach, nutrition, strength, academics), with names removed.

**The questions**
- A few **Scores**, one per dimension, for example "how does the position coach describe progress this spring?" rated on concrete 1–5 levels.
- Code combines them with weights you set by hand. With only 34 players, fitting the weights to data would overfit.

**How the answer is used**
- It fills the same trajectory field `coach_pdf.py` already prints.

**If it's uncertain, wrong or unavailable**
- Show "no clear read" instead of a number.
- Keep the Claude-pass scores as the current version.

**How to test it**
- On the same 34 players, reach ρ ≥ 0.30 and give identical answers on a second run.
- With n = 34, this can't prove Jev is better. The real payoff is a scorer that runs unchanged on next spring's notes. It's also off-season, so nothing in-season is at risk.

## Ruled out, and why

- **Tech Inventory athlete-data flag:** Jev would see only a brand name. The chartered final run is 09-29, so leave it alone.
- **Matchup injury triage:** the real work is fetching the news, which is code, not judgment.
- **Ath_Medicine themes or CATES grading:** the surgery probe failed, and whether clinical note text can be sent out is still your call.
- **Rerank, evidence tags, sde_cascade:** all already measured and dropped.

## Recommendation

**Start with #1, the Fireflies meeting tag.**
- It's the only candidate where plain code was tried first and measured short (6%).
- Something already uses the answer, and it recurs.
- When Jev is unsure, the result is exactly today's behaviour.
- The test takes you about 40 quick hand-tags.

Stopping here is also a reasonable choice. If `/meeting-prep` missing meetings doesn't actually bother you, the sandbox's own "maintenance" advice holds, and the one step worth doing regardless is to merge or close PR #21.

Nothing has been built or changed. Tell me which one to pursue, or none.

result: Three possible Jev uses; the Fireflies meeting-to-project tag is the strongest start, and stopping at maintenance is also reasonable. Nothing built.

# Workflow Expectations

- When asked to **create, merge, or consolidate an artifact** (calendar, deck, doc), the expected deliverable is always a produced file. Verify what exists first, then create the artifact regardless — never conclude with "it already exists" instead of delivering the file.
- When the user types `/graphify`, invoke the Skill tool with `skill: "graphify"` before doing anything else.

Handled by the `keystone-unified-snapshot.js` SessionStart hook — do not read these files by hand. It injects `global-memory/USER.md`, `global-memory/MEMORY.md`, `transcripts/.errors.log` (only when non-empty), and a pointer to the KeystoneOS snapshot.

- If `.errors.log` content appears, surface it once on the first response, then continue. It is normally empty; entries mean hook failures.
- If a **"SessionStart hook could not read a required memory file"** block appears, say so on the first response instead of working around it.
- **If no `## User profile` block is in context at session start, the hook did not fire.** Say so, then read `USER.md`, `MEMORY.md` and `transcripts/.errors.log` by hand.
- What the hook injects is a frozen snapshot. Mid-session writes take effect next session. Never load more than this proactively.

# Memory — routing only

The two-tier memory system (`~/.claude/global-memory/` and `~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/`) is owned by the **`memory-write` skill**, which holds the tier rules, character caps, slug rules, write steps, retrieval ladder, and daily-compiled-log rules.

The active project's Tier A memory (`~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/`, indexed by its `MEMORY.md`) is **auto-injected by the harness** each session. Tier A files are also indexed by memsearch, so they stay recallable across projects.

- Writing a fact — "remember this", "note that", "save this", "forget about" → `Skill("memory-write")`
- Recalling past context — "did we already…?", "what did we decide about X" → `Skill("memory-write")`, retrieval-ladder section
- Daily compiled logs at `~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/daily/` are owned by `claude-memory-compiler`. Never hand-edit them; never read them eagerly.
- **Slugs differ per machine** (Mac `-Users-kristinarash-DEV-<X>`, Windows `C--Users-eric-rash-Desktop-DEV-<X>`). Tier A written on one is not auto-injected on the other; memsearch still finds it. Durable project facts belong in the repo's `docs/` so both machines see them.

Do not restate the memory procedure in this file. It has one home, and that home is the skill.

---

`AGENTS.md` is the sibling of this file for harnesses that have no Skill tool (Codex and similar). It intentionally carries the memory rules as plain prose instead of routing to a skill. **The two files are not meant to be identical — do not "fix" the difference by symlinking them.**

- This is the Baylor-managed Windows laptop. Native shell is PowerShell 7 (`pwsh`) / Windows PowerShell; Claude Code hooks run under Git Bash, where `$HOME` is `/c/Users/eric_rash`.

  - No admin rights by default. Anything needing elevation (Hyper-V, diskpart, services) has to be run by Eric in an elevated PowerShell.
  - Docker Desktop (WSL2) hosts Milvus for memsearch. It must be running for memsearch hooks to work.
  - `dcg` is not installed here; the PreToolUse hook is guarded and passes through.
  - Paths with spaces are common (`G:\My Drive\...`, `OneDrive - Baylor University`). Quote them.
- DEV projects live at `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV` (one root, one repo per project; Football/ sub-projects are their own repos).
- Primary storage drive (documents, data, deliverables): `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive` (Google Drive; moved off Baylor OneDrive 2026-09-10).
- Legacy tool scripts for the migration live in `C:\DEV\_tools`.

Of the 84 meetings with named speakers, **39 map to no chartered project** — so "none of these" must be an option.
